seoTitle: How to Create an Asana Task From Email Easily
metaDescription: Turn a forwarded email into an Asana task with the project's own email address, and use To versus CC correctly to assign it instead of just notifying someone.
intro: Every Asana project has a hidden email address that turns a forwarded message into a task, a faster way to capture an action item than opening a browser tab, finding the right project, and filling out a form by hand. This guide covers finding that address, formatting the email so the subject and body land in the right fields, and using the To and CC fields correctly, since mixing them up is the most common reason an emailed task doesn't come out the way you expected.
prerequisites: You must already be a member of the destination project, or the project and its team must be public. Asana drops emailed tasks from accounts without access.

steps.heading: Open the project that should receive the task
steps.body: Start from the Asana project you want new tasks to land in, in this example a "YT Project" board organized into To do, Doing, and Done sections, with columns for Assignee, Due date, Priority, and Status. A task created by email drops into the project's default section with none of these fields set beyond the title, description, and whatever you specify through To and CC, so you'll likely move and configure it afterward.

image.caption: The destination Asana project, a To do / Doing / Done board with Assignee, Due date, Priority, and Status columns already in use.

steps.heading: Locate the project's Add Tasks via Email address
steps.body: Open the project's menu (the "..." or options icon near the project name) and look for Add Tasks via Email. Clicking it reveals a long, unique address tied specifically to that project, not your personal Asana account, and not shared across other projects. Copy it somewhere you can paste from, since you'll need it every time you want to route an email into this particular project.

steps.heading: Draft the email like you're writing to a person
steps.body:
Open your regular email client, Gmail, Outlook, whichever you already use, and start a new message addressed to the project's copied address, exactly as you'd email a colleague. No special app or plugin is required on the sending side; Asana's mail server does the parsing once the message arrives.

Write the subject as you'd want the task to read on the board: short and specific, not a full sentence. The body becomes the task description, so context, links, or instructions for whoever picks it up can go there instead of Asana's description field.

steps.heading: Assign through To, not CC
steps.body: Any extra address you add to the To field, alongside the project's own address, is set as the task's assignee. The CC field does something different: addresses there become followers, who get notified about the task but aren't assigned to it. Either way, the address has to match an existing Asana account with access to the project, or the effect silently doesn't apply.

steps.heading: Attach files, then send
steps.body: Any files attached to the email carry over and attach to the new task automatically, which makes this a fast way to log a task and hand off a reference document, a spec, a screenshot, a PDF, in the same action. Send it, then switch back to Asana and refresh the project; the new task should appear in the default section with the subject as its title and the body as its description. If nothing shows up after a minute or two, check the sender has access to the project before assuming the address was wrong.

troubleshooting.problem: The person I CC'd wasn't assigned the task.
troubleshooting.cause: CC only adds followers. Assignment happens through the To field instead.
troubleshooting.fix: Add the intended assignee's Asana-linked email address to the email's To field, alongside the project's own address.

troubleshooting.problem: Sending the email did nothing; no task ever appeared.
troubleshooting.cause: The sender usually isn't a member of that project or its team, and Asana drops mail from accounts without access unless the project and team are public.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the sender has access to the project, or make the project and team public if that fits your workspace.

troubleshooting.problem: The task appeared with no due date, priority, or status set.
troubleshooting.cause: Email-created tasks only fill in the title, description, attachments, and whoever you put in To or CC. Nothing else transfers.
troubleshooting.fix: Set those fields manually in Asana afterward, or have a rule in the project fill in common defaults for anything created this way.

faq.question: Where do I find the project's unique email address?
faq.answer: Open the project's options menu inside Asana and look for Add Tasks via Email, which reveals the project-specific address to copy.

faq.question: How do I assign the task through email?
faq.answer: Add the assignee's Asana-linked address to the To field, not CC. CC only makes someone a follower who gets notified; it doesn't assign the task.

faq.question: Can I attach files by forwarding an email?
faq.answer: Yes. Any attachments included in the email carry over and attach to the newly created task automatically.

faq.question: Does this work from any email provider?
faq.answer: Yes, from any client, including Gmail and Outlook, since it relies only on sending a message to the project's address.

faq.question: Which section of the project does the new task land in?
faq.answer: A task created by email drops into the project's default section, not one you choose, so you'll typically need to move it afterward.

verifiedNote: Click path and the board layout come from a recorded walkthrough of a real project set up to receive emailed tasks. The To-versus-CC behavior was checked against Asana's official Help Center in September 2026 and corrects the earlier draft, which had CC doing the assigning; in Asana's own documentation, To assigns and CC only adds a follower.
